source.title: Scaling Tumor Segmentation: Best Lessons from Real and Synthetic Data
source.authors: Qi Chen; Xin-Ze Zhou; Chen Liu; Hao Chen; Wen-Xuan Li; Zekun Jiang; Zi-Yan Huang; Yuxuan Zhao; Dexin Yu; Jun-Jun He; Ye-Feng Zheng; Ling Shao; Alan L. Yuille; Zong-Wei Zhou

record.file_problem: None noted; full paper and supplementary material are present.
record.tranche_reason: Applies data-scaling experiments to medical-image tumor segmentation, a different modality and task from language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: The study varies annotated tumor-data scale and reports segmentation trends, not held-out language-model cross-entropy or fitted power laws. It does not measure parameter-count, token-count, or compute scaling, extrapolation from fitted laws, or compute-optimal allocation. It does report in-distribution and out-of-distribution segmentation scaling in an image domain, relevant to V5's cross-modality scope, but does not establish whether those curves have the same power-law form. The text also cites language-model scaling laws as motivation; cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study varies the number of annotated CT scans, with and without synthetic tumors, for supervised tumor segmentation. It reports DSC, NSD and sensitivity curves, not held-out loss. It fits no power law and varies neither parameters nor compute. Its 'scaling laws' framing is motivation; the results show plateau and continued-improvement trends whose functional form is never tested. V5's claim that the same power-law form holds in other modalities therefore cannot be checked from these results. The finding is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude three things. In-distribution tumor-segmentation accuracy plateaus after about 1,500 real scans. Synthetic tumors let about 500 real scans reach the same performance, which they describe as 'steepening' the scaling curve. Out-of-distribution performance keeps improving with more, and more diverse, data. They use 'scaling laws' language loosely and fit no power laws.
record.recipe_differences: Supervised medical-image segmentation performance is measured while varying annotated tumor scans and adding synthetic tumors; no language-model loss-scaling recipe or power-law fitting is used.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported trend differs between in-distribution and out-of-distribution evaluation; it also depends on whether training uses real data alone or real plus synthetic data. The authors state that the 1,500-scan plateau is specific to pancreatic tumors in abdominal CT with the ResEncM model.

fits_no_version.finding: In supervised CT tumor segmentation, in-distribution DSC rises then plateaus with more real scans. On the proprietary set, DSC goes from 40.2 at 60 scans to 59.3 at 1,500 and 59.7 at 3,159 (Table 5). Adding 3x synthetic tumors reaches a similar level with about 278–435 real scans. Out-of-distribution DSC keeps rising (6.6 to 41.2) with real data alone.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For supervised medical-image segmentation, task-metric gains from more annotated data saturate in-distribution but continue out-of-distribution, and synthetic data shifts the curve toward fewer real samples.

record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Computer Vision
record.problems: The scaling plots do not provide extractable numeric values in the text. The supplementary proprietary-dataset scaling results are described as single experiments, and the authors say they plan to repeat experiments at least 10 times. The authors also note that the plateau result is specific to pancreatic tumors in abdominal CT with ResEncM, and that synthetic-tumor anatomical realism has not been fully verified.
record.rows_left_out: No rows retained because the reported outcomes are segmentation metrics and qualitative image-domain scaling curves, not measurements of the power-law form named by V5. Numeric scaling results appear in Figure 6, Figure 7, and Supplementary Table 5.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
Architecture shape at fixed parameter count.

Power-law form in image or other modalities. Data-size curves for CT segmentation are reported, but no loss is measured and no power-law fit is made. Video, repeated data and fine-tuning or transfer scaling are not studied.
Downstream performance vs language-model scale or pretraining loss.
Sensitivity of fitted exponents to setup or fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: Table 5 (proprietary data) gives numeric curves that a researcher could fit, but they are task metrics from single runs. The setups are inconsistent: Table 5 says SegResNet (MONAI) was used, while the conclusion attributes the 1,500-scan plateau to ResEncM. Real-only out-of-distribution patient-level sensitivity is non-monotone (100 at 60 scans, 81.5 at 3,159), so 'continues to improve' holds mainly for DSC and NSD. The reader's T3/tests classification is not adopted: no measure bears on the power-law form V5 names.

The study tests image-domain data-scaling behavior, but does not fit or test the same power-law form; it does not study video, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer as scaling regimes.
